name: Ahishar
title: Chief steward under King Solomon
summary: Ahijah was a high-ranking official at King Solomon's court who held the position of palace administrator – the one responsible for the king's household. He is mentioned in the list of Solomon's chief officials in 1 Kings 4, where he is listed with the title "the one over the house". This position entailed responsibility for the daily operations of the royal palace, including management of supplies, servant staff, and ceremonial functions. Ahijah's role illustrates the sophisticated administrative apparatus that characterized Solomon's reign and which helped consolidate the united kingdom of Israel as a regional power.

keyEvents.title: Ahishar listed as chief steward
keyEvents.description: In the list of Solomon's leading officials, Ahishar is mentioned as the one who had oversight over the king's household – one of the most central administrative positions in the kingdom.

keyEvents.title: Solomon's Administrative System
keyEvents.description: Ahishar was part of an extensive and well-organized official apparatus under Solomon, with specialized roles to ensure effective governance of the united kingdom of Israel.

versions.summary: Ahishar (also spelled Ahishar) was an official under King Solomon who served as chief steward, that is, the one who had oversight over the king's household. He is mentioned in the list of Solomon's leading officials and played an important administrative role in the united kingdom of Israel.
versions.title: Solomon's Chief Steward
versions.reason: [major] Ahijah is mentioned in 1 Kings 4:6, but some translations and the Hebrew text place him in verse 6 while others have him in verse 7. In the Hebrew text (MT), Ahijah is referred to as 'asher al-habbayit' (the one who is over the house). The verse is correctly placed as verse 6 in most translations, but this should be verified.; [minor] The role of 'leader' is very general. A more specific title such as 'chief officer' or 'official' would be more descriptive and accurate for Ahijah's function.; [minor] Verses 22–23 in 1 Kings 4 concern Solomon's daily provisions, not directly Ahijah's role. Although this may relate to the responsibilities of the chief officer, the connection is somewhat speculative since the text does not explicitly link these verses to Ahijah.; [minor] The event 'Solomon's wealth and wisdom' with reference to 1 Kings 10:23–25 is very indirectly connected to Ahijah. This event primarily concerns Solomon himself and not Ahijah specifically. Consider removing this event or making the connection clearer.; [minor] Typo: 'spillte' should be 'spilte' (one l).; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a biblical figure like Ahijah, there should be at least one footnote covering the Hebrew name, the role of chief officer ('asher al-habbayit'), and its significance in ancient Israel.

It should be rephrased to provide a fresher perspective and avoid repetition.; [minor] The third key event object ('Administration of the royal house') refers to exactly the same verse as the first (1 Kings 4:6) and largely repeats the same point. footnotes.text: The Hebrew name Ahishar (אֲחִישָׁר) is composed of אָח ('brother') and שָׁר, which can mean either 'song' or 'prince/ruler'. The name can thus be interpreted as 'my brother is a song', 'my brother is a prince', or 'brother of righteousness'. The exact etymology is debated among scholars.

The title 'asher al-habbayit' (אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַבָּיִת), meaning 'the one who is over the house', was one of the most prominent administrative positions in the Israelite kingdom. The role corresponded roughly to what we know as a steward or majordomo in later European courts. Similar titles are found in Egyptian and Mesopotamian administrative systems, suggesting that Solomon's government was shaped by established bureaucratic models in the ancient Near East.

Archaeological finds from the Iron Age, including seal impressions bearing the title 'asher al-habbayit', confirm that this was a real and important administrative position in ancient Israel and Judah. A well-known seal from around the 8th century BC, found in the Lachish area, bears this title and testifies to the continuity of the office over several centuries.

Solomon's list of officials in 1 Kings 4 attests to a thoroughly organized bureaucratic system with clearly defined areas of responsibility. This administrative structure shows clear parallels to Egyptian governance practices and marks a transition from a decentralized tribal society to a centralized monarchy in Israel.

The role of chief steward ('the one who is over the house') later also gained theological significance. In Isaiah 22:20–22, the transfer of this office from Shebna to Eliakim is used as an image of divine authority – a motif that was later interpreted messianically in Christian tradition (cf. Rev 3:7).

In rabbinic tradition, Solomon's administrative efficiency was seen as an expression of the divine wisdom he received (cf. 1 Kings 3:9–12). The appointment of competent officials like Ahishar was interpreted as a practical outworking of this wisdom in action.
